title: Local time-reversal-invariant topological markers in two dimensions
authors: Thomas Klein Kvorning, Miguel F. Martínez, Julia D. Hannukainen
abstract: Local topological markers provide a real-space characterization of topological phases and are suited to noncrystalline models. We derive a local topological marker, the Chern-Simons descendant marker, for characterizing the topology of two-dimensional time-reversal-invariant near-Gaussian states from the one-particle density matrix \(ρ\). We construct an auxiliary three-dimensional state characterized by the local Chern-Simons marker, and use dimensional reduction to obtain the Chern-Simons descendant marker for the original two-dimensional state. This derivation introduces a local Hermitian involution \(S\) that is odd under time reversal. When \([S,ρ]=0\), the local Chern-Simons descendant marker reduces to half the difference of the local Chern markers in the \(S=\pm1\) sectors. Constructing an \(S\) that commutes exactly with \(ρ\) generally requires fine-tuning, but this is not needed---the local Chern-Simon marker remains well defined whenever \(Γ=\{ρ,S\}-S\) has a spectral gap around zero, even when \([S,ρ]\neq0\). This leaves the practical problem of identifying a suitable \(S\) for a given state, which, importantly, is straightforward even when spin is not a candidate. We show this by considering both strong Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling, for which knowledge of the physical origin of the state reduces the general problem of choosing $S$ to a one-parameter family \(S(θ)\). We evaluate the optimal angle $θ$ maximizing the spectral gap of $Γ$ analytically assuming translation invariance, and find that the gap of $Γ$ remains open for a broad range of angles around the optimum. The same value of \(θ\) remains valid in disordered systems, providing an easy way to obtain choice of \(S\) for evaluating the local Chern-Simons descendant marker of the state.
summary: This work introduces the Chern-Simons descendant marker, a novel, local, and state-based tool to characterize the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological invariant in 2D time-reversal-invariant systems. It achieves this by deriving the marker from the one-particle density matrix and systematically optimizing an auxiliary operator $S$ to ensure the marker remains well-defined even in the presence of disorder. This provides a powerful, practical diagnostic tool for condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a practical, real-space, and state-based local topological marker for characterizing topological phases in two-dimensional time-reversal-invariant systems.
main_result: A local Chern-Simons descendant marker is derived directly from the one-particle density matrix, providing a robust $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant that remains well-defined even when the system is disordered or when simple commutation relations are not met.
method: The marker is obtained via dimensional reduction from an auxiliary three-dimensional state, requiring the identification and optimization of a local Hermitian involution $S$ that maximizes the spectral gap of an associated operator $\Gamma$.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on two-dimensional time-reversal-invariant near-Gaussian states, utilizing the one-particle density matrix $\rho$ as the primary input. The method is tested in models exhibiting strong Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling.
key_observables: Local Chern-Simons descendant marker, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant, spectral gap of $\Gamma$, one-particle density matrix ($\rho$).
important_parameters: The optimal angle $\theta$ used to define the involution $S$, which is shown to be robust across different physical regimes.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the properties of Gaussian states and the assumption that the spectral gap condition on $\Gamma$ is the key requirement for the marker's definition, rather than exact commutation $[S, \rho]=0$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of local topological markers, derives the Chern-Simons descendant marker through dimensional reduction, and details the systematic procedure for selecting and optimizing the auxiliary operator $S$ by maximizing the spectral gap of $\Gamma$.
why_interesting: The development of a local, measurable marker for topological invariants in disordered systems is crucial for understanding real-world materials where perfect crystalline order is absent, bridging abstract topology with measurable physical quantities.
